strengths: Compelling and intuitive conceptual hypothesis inspired by cognitive development: learning generalized manipulation by mastering composable geometric primitives ('Cézanne toys').

Impressive real-world experimental effort: 3D-printing 250 distinct primitive-composed toys, gathering 1,500 real Franka demonstrations and 500 humanoid dexterous hand demonstrations, and evaluating across 64 YCB objects with 16 trials per object (over 1,000 physical trials per evaluated system).
Thorough ablation and scaling analysis investigating the trade-offs between toy variety, demonstration density, primitive composition, and transformer model capacity.

The proposed DetPool mechanism is simple, intuitive, and clearly demonstrates strong improvements over standard token pooling techniques (CLS, mean, attention pooling) for out-of-distribution visual transfer.
weaknesses: Comparison missing dedicated 3D grasp pose estimation baselines: While the paper thoroughly compares against modern generalist VLA policies (OpenVLA, π0-FAST), standard open-world zero-shot grasping methods (e.g., AnyGrasp, Contact-GraspNet, or GraspNet-1B) are standard baselines for zero-shot YCB grasping and are not benchmarked.

Reliance on an external segmentation pipeline: In real-world deployment, DetPool depends on an upstream Faster R-CNN object detector and SAM 2. The pipeline's robustness in cluttered multi-object scenes or cases where target segmentation fails is not thoroughly analyzed.

Simplicity of the manipulation task: The evaluation is strictly restricted to isolated, tabletop single-object grasping and lifting. How well the primitive-composition paradigm extends to contact-rich, pre-grasp repositioning or tool-use behaviors remains an open question.

Inconsistent evaluation thresholds: In Appendix H.1, the lifting success height threshold for OpenVLA-OFT in simulation was lowered from 0.3 m to 0.15 m due to premature gripper opening. While intended to be lenient to the baseline, evaluation criteria should remain uniform across all methods.

strengths: Intriguing conceptual hypothesis inspired by developmental psychology: showing that training manipulation policies on randomly composed geometric primitives ('Cézanne toys') allows zero-shot generalization to unseen real-world objects.

Substantial physical and experimental effort: designing, 3D-printing 250 physical toys across 8 printers, teleoperating demonstrations, and evaluating across 64 real YCB objects on a Franka Panda, as well as testing on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot with dexterous hands.
Systematic ablations exploring scaling properties (number of unique toys vs. number of demonstrations), the contribution of individual shape primitives, and toy complexity.

DetPool provides a simple and effective mechanism to focus ViT representations onto object regions, yielding consistent performance improvements over standard pooling alternatives (mean, CLS, attention pooling).
weaknesses: Missing comparisons to established generalizable grasping pipelines: The paper compares exclusively against generalist VLA models (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST) and ShapeGrasp, but omits well-established 6-DoF grasp generation methods (e.g., Contact-GraspNet, AnyGrasp, or Dex-Net) which are strong and standard benchmarks for zero-shot object grasping.

Technical novelty of DetPool is relatively limited: Restricting ViT attention to foreground segmentation masks (obtained via Faster R-CNN and SAM 2) and performing mean pooling over masked tokens is a known technique in vision and object-centric learning.

Pipeline dependency and evaluation details: Real-world execution requires a multi-stage perception pipeline (annotated Faster R-CNN detector + SAM 2) before DetPool can operate, but the sensitivity to mask quality or tracking errors during approach/grasping is not thoroughly analyzed.

In real robot experiments, fine-tuned π0-FAST outperforms the proposed approach on the Franka Panda benchmark (76.56% vs. 66.67%), somewhat qualifying the claim of outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.
Humanoid robot experiments (Unitree H1-2) are evaluated on a limited test suite (13 objects, 5 trials each) under acknowledged hardware degradation (e.g., unresponsive thumb joints).

strengths: Compelling conceptual premise: Inspiring robot learning from developmental cognitive science (infants learning manipulation via basic toys) and Cézanne's geometric decomposition to study out-of-distribution generalization is creative and well-motivated.

Impressive hardware and physical experiment effort: The authors manufactured 250 physical 3D-printed toys across diverse primitive compositions, teleoperated physical demonstrations (Franka Panda and Unitree H1-2 humanoid), and conducted extensive physical evaluations on YCB objects and everyday items.

Thorough empirical analysis and scaling studies: The paper provides informative ablations dissecting how zero-shot transfer scales with object count, demo count, primitive types (e.g., finding spheres most critical), toy complexity, and network capacity.

Data efficiency: Demonstrates that an object-centric inductive bias (DetPool) allows a compact model (86M parameters) to achieve competitive grasping success without requiring internet-scale pretraining datasets.
weaknesses: Missing specialized grasping baselines: The paper compares exclusively against generalist VLA models (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST) and an LLM-based method (ShapeGrasp). However, modular 6-DoF grasp synthesis methods (e.g., AnyGrasp, Contact-GraspNet, Dex-Net) are standard, highly competitive baselines for zero-shot rigid object grasping on tabletops and should be benchmarked or discussed.

Subtle overclaiming regarding baseline comparison: The abstract and introduction state that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches; however, in Table 2, π0-FAST fine-tuned on the toy demonstrations achieves 76.56%, notably outperforming LEGO's 66.67%. The zero-shot π0-FAST without toy tuning also achieves 61.82%, which is quite close.

Modest technical novelty of Detection Pooling (DetPool): DetPool essentially consists of applying SAM 2 to generate an object mask, using that mask to restrict self-attention inside the ViT, and average pooling the object tokens. Object-centric attention masking and masked pooling are standard techniques in visual representation learning.

Compromised dexterous hand evaluation: As noted in Appendix H.3, technical issues with the Inspire hands (unresponsive thumb joints) impacted the execution of dexterous grasping. Clarification is needed on whether the hand was functionally acting as an underactuated caging/pinching device rather than performing true dexterous grasping.

Reliance on 2D segmentation: The policy strongly relies on upstream 2D object segmentation (Faster R-CNN + SAM 2). In cluttered, occluded, or visually ambiguous tabletop environments, segmentation failures or multi-instance ambiguities could significantly hinder real-world performance.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Inspired by cognitive development and geometric abstraction, the paper explores whether robots can learn generalizable manipulation skills solely by interacting with randomly assembled shape primitives ('Cézanne toys'). This offers an interesting and data-efficient counterpoint to brute-force web-scale pretraining.

Impressive real-world execution: The authors physically manufactured 250 unique 3D-printed toys and collected real robot demonstrations across two distinct hardware embodiments (Franka Panda arm with parallel gripper and Unitree H1-2 humanoid with 6-DoF dexterous hands).

Strong empirical performance and sample efficiency: Trained on only 1,500 real demonstrations on synthetic toys, an 86M parameter policy achieves a 66.7% zero-shot success rate across 64 real YCB objects, outperforming several large pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines such as OpenVLA-OFT and zero-shot π0-FAST.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and ablations: The manuscript features extensive scaling analyses across dataset size, object diversity, model parameter scale, primitive ablation, toy complexity, and robustness to lighting, scene clutter, and segmentation mask noise.
weaknesses: Omission of specialized zero-shot grasping baselines: While the comparison against generalist VLAs (π0-FAST, OpenVLA-OFT) is informative, the paper lacks comparisons against established geometric and affordance-based grasp planners (e.g., Contact-GraspNet, AnyGrasp, GraspNet-1B) which are standard benchmarks for open-vocabulary/zero-shot rigid object picking.

Reliance on external segmentation/detection pipelines: The proposed Detection Pooling (DetPool) module relies on accurate target masks from SAM 2 and a trained Faster R-CNN detector. In densely cluttered, heavily occluded, or visually ambiguous real-world environments, segmentation failure modes directly propagate to manipulation failures.

Task scope primarily limited to top-down / simple picking: While an appendix experiment touches on planar pushing, the evaluation centers predominantly on rigid, isolated object picking. Generalization to articulated mechanisms, deformables, or functional/tool-use grasping remains unverified.

Discrepancies in baseline control representations: The paper notes that LEGO adopts absolute joint position control, whereas baselines like OpenVLA-OFT were evaluated under delta control settings (and OpenVLA received a lowered lifting height threshold in simulation). Ensuring completely symmetric control spaces would make baseline comparisons even more rigorous.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated conceptual premise: drawing inspiration from cognitive developmental literature and Cézanne's geometric decomposition to train generalizable grasping policies using only randomly assembled 3D shape primitives (spheres, cuboids, cylinders, rings).

Impressive real-world experimental effort: the authors 3D-printed 250 custom procedural toys, collected 1,500 real Franka teleoperation demonstrations and 500 humanoid teleoperation demonstrations, and conducted extensive physical evaluations on 64 YCB objects (16 trials per object) as well as dexterous humanoid grasping.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations: the paper compares against relevant baselines (π0-FAST, OpenVLA-OFT, ShapeGrasp, DexGraspVLA, GROOT) and conducts detailed ablations across pooling mechanisms (DetPool vs. CLS/mean/attention pooling), scaling behavior (number of toys vs. demos), primitive composition, visual clutter, lighting variation, and segmentation noise.

Detection Pooling (DetPool) is simple, modular, and empirically effective: constraining the ViT's self-attention to target object patches provides a clear mechanism to prevent background/context overfitting and enables zero-shot OOD generalization.
weaknesses: Limited task scope and lack of semantic awareness: the method is essentially focused on primitive-guided tabletop grasping (with a preliminary push experiment in the appendix). Because the policy operates purely on the segmented object mask, it lacks semantic conditioning to select between multiple everyday items unless guided by an external upstream detector.

Reliance on an external perception pipeline: DetPool depends heavily on generating accurate object masks (Faster R-CNN + SAM 2 in real-world experiments). In complex real-world scenes with heavy occlusion, transparent objects, or poor contrast, failure in the upstream segmentation directly propagates to policy failure.

Nuance in baseline comparisons: on the real Franka robot benchmark (Table 2), finetuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56% success, clearly surpassing LEGO's 66.67%. While LEGO is trained from scratch with 86M parameters (vs. 3B parameters + extensive pretraining for π0), the claim of outperforming state-of-the-art approaches should be qualified more carefully.

Ad-hoc baseline evaluation criteria: in Appendix I.1, the success height threshold for OpenVLA-OFT in simulation was lowered from 0.3m to 0.15m because its gripper opened prematurely. Modifying the metric post-hoc for specific baselines is irregular and should be avoided or clearly standardized.

strengths: Compelling and intuitive core hypothesis: learning to manipulate random compositions of basic geometric shapes ('Cézanne toys') can enable effective zero-shot transfer to real-world everyday objects.

Extensive real-robot experimentation: 3D printing 250 physical toys, collecting teleoperated demonstrations on both a 7-DoF Franka Panda and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with 6-DoF dexterous hands, and evaluating across 64 real YCB objects and 13 everyday objects.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and ablations: includes scaling laws regarding the number of toys vs. demonstrations, primitive type importance, complexity scaling, Chamfer distance correlation, prediction horizon, and robustness against clutter, lighting, and mask noise.
weaknesses: Limited baseline selection for grasping: The evaluation primarily compares LEGO against large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (OpenVLA, π0-FAST) and ShapeGrasp. However, for tabletop grasping and zero-shot transfer, dedicated grasp synthesis / affordance learning baselines (e.g., AnyGrasp, Contact-GraspNet, Dex-Net) are standard benchmarks and notably absent.

Potential confounding factors and discrepancies in baseline configurations: In Appendix C.5, the authors demonstrate that delta control plateaus severely (30–37%) compared to absolute joint control (up to 80%). Yet, as detailed in Appendix H, OpenVLA-OFT was trained and evaluated using delta joint position control, which may have substantially handicapped its performance.

Technical novelty of the model architecture is modest: Detection Pooling (DetPool) is essentially applying an attention mask using an off-the-shelf segmenter (SAM 2) to attend only to foreground object patch tokens within a standard ViT, followed by mean pooling. Masked attention and object-centric pooling are standard techniques in vision and robotics.

Unclear real-world detection pipeline: Appendix F notes that for real-world setups, a Faster R-CNN detector was trained on 200 toy images to produce bounding boxes for SAM 2. It is unclear how well this detector generalizes class-agnostically to the 64 novel real YCB objects and clutter/distractors without missing objects or false proposals.
